lessons.title: The patient care report, start to finish
lessons.body:
## What the report is for

The patient care report (PCR) is four documents wearing one coat: a **clinical handoff**, a **legal record**, a **billing document**, and a **data submission** to the state and national EMS databases. A complete report serves all four at once.

## The minimum data set

**Run data**: unit, crew and certification levels, times for dispatch, en route, on scene, patient contact, departure, arrival, and transfer of care, plus mileage and destination. **Patient data**: demographics, chief complaint, history, all vitals with times, all interventions with times and responses, and who accepted care.

Times are the spine. A case reviewed years later is reconstructed entirely from them.

## Two narrative formats

**CHART**: Chief complaint, History, Assessment, Rx (treatment), Transport.
**SOAP**: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan.

Pick one and use it every time so nothing gets dropped under pressure.

## Example 1: a medical call in CHART format

"**C:** Dispatched `1847`, unresponsive person. Patient contact `1854`. `54`-year-old male on the floor against a couch; wife reports he became confused over `20` minutes then stopped answering her.

**H:** Type 1 diabetes on an insulin pump, hypertension. Medications insulin, lisinopril. No known allergies. Last oral intake breakfast `0800`, skipped lunch. Two prior low-sugar episodes this month. No trauma witnessed.

**A:** Airway patent, snoring relieved with a jaw thrust. Breathing `16` and adequate, lungs clear. Skin cool and diaphoretic, radial pulse `104` regular. Responds to painful stimulus only (AVPU P). Pupils `3 mm` equal and reactive. Glucose `32 mg/dL`. No trauma found on rapid head-to-toe. Vitals `1856`: HR `104`, BP `138/84`, RR `16`, SpO2 `96%` room air.

**Rx:** Nasopharyngeal airway `28 Fr` placed `1857`. Oxygen `4 L` nasal cannula `1857`. Oral glucose withheld due to inability to protect airway. ALS intercept requested `1855`. Responsive to voice `1908` after ALS dextrose; repeat glucose `112 mg/dL` at `1912`. Vitals `1912`: HR `88`, BP `132/80`, RR `16`, SpO2 `98%`, oriented times four. Patient states, 'I must have bolused twice.'

**T:** Transported non-emergent to County General, semi-Fowler, reassessed every `5` minutes. Arrived `1926`. Care transferred `1929` to RN M. Boateng, bed 12, verbal report given. Insulin pump left in place and reported to receiving nurse."

## Example 2: a trauma call in CHART format

"**C:** Dispatched `1412`, fall from a roof. Patient contact `1421`. `38`-year-old male fell approximately `18` feet onto grass, witnessed by a coworker. In his words: 'My back is killing me and my leg is bent wrong.'

**H:** No known history, no medications, no allergies. Last oral intake `1200`. Coworker reports no loss of consciousness.

**A:** Supine on grass, airway patent, speaking full sentences. Breathing `24`, chest symmetrical, lungs clear at four points, no crepitus. Radial pulse `118` weak, skin pale and cool, capillary refill `3` seconds. Oriented times four, GCS `15`. Rapid head-to-toe: `6 cm` abrasion right forearm; midline tenderness at the lower thoracic spine; abdomen soft; pelvis stable on single palpation; mid-shaft right femur deformity with a `2 cm` open wound, dark bleeding controlled by direct pressure, distal pulse and sensation intact. Log roll: no posterior wounds. Vitals `1424`: HR `118`, BP `112/86`, RR `24`, SpO2 `95%`. Vitals `1436`: HR `126`, BP `104/88`, RR `26`, SpO2 `97%` on `15 L`.

**Rx:** Manual in-line stabilization from contact, collar `1424`. Oxygen `15 L` non-rebreather `1425`. Sterile dressing and direct pressure to right thigh `1426`, controlled without tourniquet. Vacuum splint `1430`. Two blankets `1431`. Trauma alert `1428`. Scene departure `1433`, scene time `12` minutes due to terrain access.

**T:** Emergent to Regional Trauma Center, `9` minutes, reassessed every `5` minutes. Narrowing pulse pressure and rising heart rate reported en route. Arrived `1442`. Care transferred `1445` to the trauma team, Dr. Nakamura, trauma bay 2."

## What the billing side needs

Without editorializing, the chart must support **medical necessity**: why this patient required ambulance transport rather than another means. "Unable to ambulate due to open femur deformity" does that. Obtain a signature where required, and document the reason when you cannot.

> **Key:** One narrative format, every time, with a time attached to every vital sign, intervention, and transfer.

> **On the exam:** Falsification questions have exactly one right answer. You never document something that did not happen, even when the protocol says it should have.
keyPoints: A PCR serves four audiences at once: clinical handoff, legal record, billing document, and state and national data submission.
The minimum data set is run data plus patient data, and times are the spine of both.
CHART is chief complaint, history, assessment, Rx, transport; SOAP is subjective, objective, assessment, plan.
Every medication and intervention needs a time and a documented response, including interventions withheld and why.
Medical necessity is documented by stating why ambulance transport was required, without editorializing.

checks.q: Which best documents why oral glucose was not given to an unresponsive hypoglycemic patient?
choices: Patient refused oral glucose
Oral glucose withheld due to inability to protect airway
Oral glucose not indicated
No glucose available
checks.why: It records the clinical reason for withholding, which protects the patient and the provider. A withheld intervention with a reason is itself an assessment finding.

checks.q: What does CHART stand for?
choices: Complaint, History, Assessment, Rx, Transport
Care, History, Airway, Response, Time
Chief complaint, Hazards, Assessment, Records, Transfer
Call, Hospital, Airway, Report, Times
checks.why: CHART organizes the narrative as chief complaint, history, assessment, treatment, and transport. Using one format every time prevents dropped sections.

checks.q: A protocol says all trauma patients receive oxygen, but you did not apply it. What do you document?
choices: That oxygen was applied, to match the protocol
Nothing about oxygen at all
What actually happened, and the reason if there was one
That the patient refused oxygen
checks.why: Documenting an intervention you did not perform is falsification and ends careers. Record what happened and the clinical reason if you had one.

lessons.title: Negligence and consent: eight cases
lessons.body:
## Learn the law by running the cases

The elements are short: negligence needs **duty, breach, damages, and causation**, all four. Consent needs an informed patient with **capacity**, or an emergency that triggers **implied consent**. Everything below applies those two frameworks. Decide before you read the analysis.

## Case 1: the missed glucose

An EMT responds to a "drunk" 40-year-old, does no glucose check, and leaves him with police. He is found unresponsive in a cell four hours later with a glucose of `28 mg/dL` and suffers permanent brain injury.

**Analysis:** Duty existed on a dispatched call. Breach, because the standard of care requires a glucose on altered patients. Damages are clear. Causation is arguable but strong. All four elements are present.

## Case 2: the rude but correct EMT

An EMT is sarcastic and dismissive throughout a call but performs every assessment and treatment correctly. The patient complains.

**Analysis:** Duty yes, breach of professional conduct arguably, but no damages caused by any clinical failure. Negligence is not established. This is a complaint and possibly a disciplinary matter, not a tort.

## Case 3: the refusal with no risk conversation

A competent adult declines transport after a head strike. The EMT has him sign the form, writes "pt refused, AAOx4," and leaves. He dies of a subdural bleed overnight.

**Analysis:** Duty yes. Breach, because the standard requires a documented capacity determination, a specific risk conversation, alternatives offered, and medical direction contact for a high-risk refusal. Damages and causation follow. The signature does not save the chart, because the chart never shows that he was informed.

## Case 4: the downgrade handoff

A paramedic with a patient on a cardiac monitor receiving IV medication hands the patient to a BLS crew for the remainder of the transport.

**Analysis:** Abandonment. Transfer must be to an equal or higher level when the patient's needs exceed the receiving level's scope. Direction of transfer, not convenience, is the test.

## Case 5: the unconscious patient with no family

A 30-year-old is pulled unconscious from a crash. No family, no identification, no way to ask.

**Analysis:** Implied consent. The law presumes a reasonable person would want lifesaving care in an emergency. It covers only what the emergency requires.

## Case 6: the patient who says no and is treated anyway

A competent adult clearly declines an IV and an EMT proceeds anyway "because he needs it."

**Analysis:** **Battery**, the unlawful touching without consent. Had the EMT only threatened it, that would be **assault**. If the patient were then transported against his will, add **false imprisonment**. Good intentions are not a defense.

## Case 7: the off-duty stop

An off-duty EMT stops at a crash, provides care within her training, accepts no payment, and the patient later sues over an imperfect splint.

**Analysis:** Good Samaritan protection generally applies: voluntary, good faith, no expectation of payment, within the scope of training. Had she performed something far outside her training and made the injury worse, that could be gross negligence, which the statutes generally do not cover.

## Case 8: the doctor on scene

A bystander physician on a scene directs an EMT to perform something outside the EMT's protocol.

**Analysis:** You work under your medical director. The general approach is to contact online medical direction and let the physicians resolve it. A bystander physician who wishes to direct care is usually required to show credentials, accept responsibility, and accompany the patient. You never exceed your scope regardless of who asks.

> **Key:** Damages and causation are where most negligence claims fail. Breach without harm is a quality problem, not a lawsuit.

> **Trap:** "The patient signed" and "a doctor told me to" are the two most common false comforts in EMS. Neither substitutes for a documented process or a legal scope.

> **On the exam:** If a vignette describes an error with no patient harm, negligence is not established because damages are missing.
keyPoints: Negligence requires duty, breach, damages, and causation, and most real claims fail on damages or causation.
A refusal signature without a documented capacity determination and risk conversation does not protect anyone.
Handing a patient to a lower level of training than their needs require is abandonment.
Treating a competent adult who has refused is battery; threatening it is assault; transporting them is false imprisonment.
A bystander physician cannot expand your scope; contact online medical direction and let the physicians resolve it.

checks.q: An EMT skips a required step but the patient suffers no harm of any kind. Is negligence established?
choices: Yes, because the standard of care was breached
No, because damages are absent
Yes, because duty existed
Only if the patient complains
checks.why: All four elements must be present. Breach without resulting harm is a quality and discipline issue, not a negligence claim.

checks.q: A paramedic transfers a patient on an IV infusion and a cardiac monitor to an EMT crew mid-transport. What is this?
choices: An appropriate resource decision
Abandonment, because the transfer is to a lower level than the patient requires
Permitted with online medical direction approval only
Battery
checks.why: Transfer must be to an equal or higher level when the patient's needs exceed the receiving provider's scope. The direction of the transfer is what makes it abandonment.

checks.q: A bystander physician orders an intervention outside your protocol. What is the correct action?
choices: Perform it, since a physician is present
Refuse and ignore the physician entirely
Contact online medical direction and let the physicians resolve it, staying within your scope
Perform it only if the physician rides along
checks.why: You practice under your medical director's authority, and a bystander physician cannot expand your legal scope. Online medical direction is the mechanism to resolve it.

lessons.title: Second pass on MCI: SALT and hospital notification
lessons.body:
## Why another triage system exists

START was built in the 1980s and is fast, but it sorts on physiology alone and it has no formal step for the handful of interventions that actually save lives during sorting. **SALT** was developed as a national consensus model and is now the system many agencies teach. It stands for **Sort, Assess, Lifesaving interventions, Treatment and transport**.

## Step 1: Sort with your voice

Two commands from a place everyone can hear.

1. "Everyone who can hear me and needs help, walk to the area by the flagged truck." Those who walk are assessed **third**.
2. "Everyone who can hear me, wave your arm or move a leg." Those who wave or move purposefully are assessed **second**.
3. Everyone still and silent, or with an obvious life threat, is assessed **first**.

That is the whole difference in philosophy: SALT sorts by who is most likely to be dying right now, rather than by who can walk.

## Step 2: Assess individually, with lifesaving interventions

During individual assessment you may perform a short list, and only if it takes seconds and supplies are at hand:

- Control **major hemorrhage** (pressure, tourniquet, wound packing)
- Open the **airway** by positioning; for a child, give **2 rescue breaths**
- **Chest decompression** and **auto-injector antidotes** by providers whose scope includes them

## Step 3: Categorize

Ask in order:

- Breathing after the airway is opened? If no, **Dead** (black).
- If breathing: does the patient obey commands or make purposeful movements, have a peripheral pulse, have no severe respiratory distress, and have major bleeding controlled?
  - **All yes, and injuries are minor:** **Minimal** (green).
  - **All yes, injuries not minor:** **Delayed** (yellow).
  - **Any no:** **Immediate** (red), unless survival is unlikely given the resources available, in which case **Expectant** (gray).

The gray **expectant** category is SALT's other distinctive feature. Expectant patients are not abandoned. They receive comfort care and are reassessed as resources arrive, and an expectant patient in a small incident may be a red patient in a large one. The category is a statement about resources, not about worth.

## Hospital notification, step by step

The transport officer's job is to keep one hospital from absorbing the whole incident. The pattern, which varies by region and protocol:

1. **One early notification** through dispatch or the regional medical coordination point, with the incident type, the location, the estimated total patients, and a rough count by category.
2. **Ask each receiving facility for capacity by category**, not a general "can you take patients." The answer you want sounds like "two immediate, four delayed, ten minimal."
3. **Distribute deliberately.** Send immediates to the closest appropriate center, spread delayed patients, and route minimal patients to farther or smaller facilities.
4. **Track every patient:** tag number, category, transporting unit, and destination, recorded as each unit leaves.
5. **Update the hospitals** when the count changes, especially when the number of immediates grows.
6. **Expect uncounted arrivals.** In real incidents a large share of the walking wounded reach the nearest hospital on their own, by car or on foot, before your first ambulance arrives. Warn the closest facility about that specifically.

> **Key:** SALT sorts by who is dying now, allows a short list of lifesaving interventions during triage, and adds an expectant category tied to available resources.

> **Trap:** Sending everyone to the closest hospital is the most common failure of MCI transport, and it converts one disaster scene into two.

> **On the exam:** Know both systems. START's red thresholds are a rate over `30`, absent radial pulse or capillary refill over `2` seconds, and failure to follow commands. SALT's categories are immediate, delayed, minimal, expectant, and dead.
keyPoints: SALT is Sort, Assess, Lifesaving interventions, Treatment and transport.
Sorting uses two voice commands: walk to an area, then wave or move; the still and silent are assessed first.
Permitted interventions during SALT are hemorrhage control, airway positioning with 2 rescue breaths for a child, chest decompression, and auto-injector antidotes.
SALT categories are immediate, delayed, minimal, expectant, and dead; expectant is a resource judgment that is revisited.
Hospital notification asks for capacity by category and deliberately spreads patients, expecting self-transported walking wounded at the nearest facility.

checks.q: Under SALT, which group is assessed first?
choices: The patients who walked to the designated area
The patients who waved or moved purposefully
The patients who are still and silent or have an obvious life threat
The youngest patients
checks.why: SALT sorts by who is most likely dying now. Those who neither walk nor wave are assessed first, then wavers, then walkers.

checks.q: Which intervention is permitted during SALT individual assessment?
choices: Applying a tourniquet to control major hemorrhage
Splinting a femur fracture
Starting an IV line
Administering oxygen by non-rebreather
checks.why: SALT permits hemorrhage control, airway positioning with rescue breaths for children, chest decompression, and auto-injector antidotes. Splints, IVs, and oxygen are treatment, not triage.

checks.q: Why does the transport officer ask hospitals for capacity by category?
choices: To satisfy billing requirements
Because 'can you take patients' does not tell you how many immediates a facility can absorb
To determine ambulance staffing
To decide which patients get tagged
checks.why: A hospital may have room for ten minimal patients and only one immediate. Category-specific capacity is what prevents overwhelming a single trauma resource.

lessons.title: Decontamination and CBRNE recognition in depth
lessons.body:
## Decontamination is a process, not a hose

The goal is to reduce the dose of contaminant on the patient to the point where care can proceed without contaminating rescuers, the ambulance, or the hospital. It runs in the **warm zone**, between the hot zone and the clean cold zone, and it moves in one direction only.

## The sequence

1. **Triage at the decon entry.** Ambulatory and non-ambulatory patients go through separate corridors, because carrying a patient through a decon line consumes four people.
2. **Remove clothing.** This is the single highest-yield step, eliminating roughly **80 to 90 percent** of the contaminant. Cut clothing away rather than pulling it over the head. Bag and tag clothing and personal effects; they are also evidence in a criminal release.
3. **Brush off dry material first.** Some dry chemicals react violently with water. Brush, then flush.
4. **Flush with copious low-pressure warm water**, head to toe, for several minutes. High pressure drives contaminant into skin, and cold water causes hypothermia in a naked patient, which is one of the most common complications of mass decontamination.
5. **Wash with mild soap** for oily or adherent agents, paying attention to hair, skin folds, and under the nails.
6. **Irrigate eyes** with water or saline. Contact lenses come out.
7. **Dry and cover.** Warm blankets, a clean gown or a Tyvek suit, and a new set of hands at the clean end.
8. **Reassess and treat.** Only in the cold zone. Move the patient to clean equipment; do not bring a stretcher through decon and then use it for the next call.

Throughout, remember that decon delays care. For a critically injured patient in a chemical event, gross decontamination, meaning clothing removal and a rapid rinse, is what happens, and the fine detail waits.

## CBRNE, recognized by pattern

**Chemical.** Sudden onset, many patients, same symptoms, in one geographic area, often with an odor or visible vapor.

- **Nerve agents** produce **SLUDGEM**: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, gastrointestinal distress, emesis, and miosis. Pinpoint pupils plus wet everything plus seizures across multiple patients is the classic picture. Antidote is an atropine and pralidoxime auto-injector kit, given by providers whose scope allows it.
- **Vesicants** such as mustard cause delayed blistering, sometimes hours later, with a garlic or mustard odor.
- **Blood agents** such as cyanide cause rapid collapse and gasping respirations with skin that stays pink; a bitter almond odor is detectable by only some people.
- **Pulmonary agents** such as chlorine and phosgene cause burning eyes and throat and delayed pulmonary edema. Chlorine smells like bleach and is **heavier than air**, so it collects in low ground and basements.

**Biological.** No scene, no odor, and no simultaneous onset. Instead you see an unusual disease cluster over days, or an unusual number of similar complaints on consecutive shifts. Suspicion often begins with an astute clinician, not a placard.

**Radiological and nuclear.** Time, distance, and shielding are the three protections. Minimize time near the source, maximize distance, and put mass between you and it. Radiation is not contagious, and an irradiated patient who has been decontaminated poses little risk to you. A **dirty bomb** is conventional explosive plus radioactive material, so the blast injuries are the immediate threat.

**Explosive.** The most likely terrorism modality. Blast injury comes in four phases: primary from the pressure wave hitting air-filled organs such as lungs, ears, and bowel; secondary from flying fragments, which causes the most casualties; tertiary from the body being thrown; quaternary from burns, crush, and inhalation.

## Staying alive as a responder

**Secondary devices** are placed to kill responders and are timed for your arrival, often at the obvious command post or staging area. So: approach from upwind, do not cluster, park somewhere other than the natural spot, do not touch unattended objects, and have law enforcement sweep before crews commit.

> **Key:** Clothing removal does most of the work. Dry brush before water, low pressure, warm water, one direction only.

> **On the exam:** Multiple patients with pinpoint pupils and copious secretions is a nerve agent. Chlorine is heavier than air and collects low. Secondary devices target responders.
keyPoints: Decon runs in the warm zone, moves one direction, and uses separate ambulatory and non-ambulatory corridors.
Removing clothing eliminates 80 to 90 percent of contaminant; brush dry material before flushing.
Flush with copious low-pressure warm water; high pressure drives contaminant in and cold water causes hypothermia.
Nerve agents produce SLUDGEM with pinpoint pupils; chlorine is heavier than air and pools in low areas.
Blast injury has four phases, and secondary devices are deliberately aimed at responders and staging areas.

checks.q: Which decontamination step removes the most contaminant?
choices: Soap scrubbing of the skin
Removal of the patient's clothing
Eye irrigation
High-pressure water rinse
checks.why: Clothing removal eliminates roughly 80 to 90 percent of the contaminant and is the first thing done after triage at the decon entry.

checks.q: Four patients from the same basement have pinpoint pupils, copious secretions, and are vomiting. What should you suspect?
choices: Mass hysteria
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Nerve agent exposure
Norovirus outbreak
checks.why: SLUDGEM with miosis across multiple patients is a nerve agent until proven otherwise. Back out, isolate, deny entry, and call a hazmat response.

checks.q: Which blast injury phase causes the most casualties in a typical explosion?
choices: Primary, from the pressure wave
Secondary, from flying fragments
Tertiary, from the body being thrown
Quaternary, from burns
checks.why: Fragmentation injuries from debris and shrapnel produce the largest number of casualties, even though primary blast injury to air-filled organs is the most distinctive.

lessons.title: Ambulance crashes: the data and the rules
lessons.body:
## The most dangerous part of the job is the drive

Transportation incidents are consistently among the leading causes of EMS line-of-duty deaths. National estimates put ambulance crashes in the range of **4,500 to 6,500 per year** in the United States, producing roughly **30** fatal crashes annually and thousands of injuries. The pattern inside those numbers is what matters.

- The **majority of serious ambulance crashes occur during emergency use**, with lights and siren running.
- **Intersections** account for a disproportionate share, and the typical crash is a vehicle entering against a red light or turning across the ambulance's path.
- The **patient compartment is the most dangerous seat**. Occupant deaths and serious injuries are concentrated among unrestrained rear occupants, who become projectiles in a collision.
- The **wake effect**, meaning crashes that happen behind you among drivers reacting to your passage, is real. Some studies suggest these may be more numerous than ambulance crashes themselves.
- **Backing collisions** are the most frequent crash type overall, and they are almost entirely preventable.

Set against that: emergency response and transport save on average only about **1.7 to 3.6 minutes** on a typical call. A handful of patients, such as those in cardiac arrest or with a time-critical stroke or major trauma, may benefit. Most do not.

## The rules that prevent the crashes in that data

**At every intersection:**

1. Come to a **complete stop** at every red light and stop sign, even with lights and siren.
2. Clear it **lane by lane**, waiting for each lane's traffic to stop.
3. Make eye contact with drivers before you enter their lane.
4. **Change the siren tone** as you approach; a constant tone becomes background noise.
5. Assume you are invisible and inaudible. Modern cars are sealed, insulated, and loud inside.

**Speed.** Excessive speed is the second half of most crash reports. Many agencies cap emergency response at the posted limit or a small margin over it, and the honest math is that `10` extra miles per hour over a `5`-mile response buys well under a minute while raising stopping distance substantially.

**Restraints and secured equipment.** Everyone belted, including the provider in the patient compartment whenever possible. Monitors, oxygen cylinders, and bags secured; an unsecured monitor in a `30` mile-per-hour crash carries the force of a small motorcycle. Newer ambulance patient compartments built to current standards use forward-facing, crash-tested seating with restraints, precisely because side-facing bench seats performed badly in testing.

**Backing.** A spotter at the rear corner, visible in your mirror, with agreed hand signals. **Stop the instant you lose sight of the spotter.** With no spotter, get out and walk the path first, every time.

**Fatigue.** Do not drive at the end of a long shift without considering whether you should. Fatigue impairs reaction time comparably to alcohol, and the commute home after a night shift is itself a documented risk.

## Deciding when to run hot

A growing number of systems use tiered dispatch to send most calls without lights and siren, and to transport without them unless a time-critical intervention is waiting. The questions to ask: will minutes change this patient's outcome, and is there an intervention at the hospital that the clock actually affects? If the answer to either is no, drive normally.

> **Key:** Lights and sirens grant exemptions, never immunity. The legal standard is due regard, and the practical standard is a complete stop at every red light.

> **Trap:** "I had the right of way" is not a defense. Exemptions are conditional on driving with due regard, and a crash is evaluated against what a reasonable operator would have done.

> **On shift:** Whoever is riding in back should be belted and should say so out loud. Normalizing the unbelted rear compartment is how crews get hurt in otherwise survivable crashes.
keyPoints: Ambulance crashes number roughly 4,500 to 6,500 a year in the US, with about 30 fatal, concentrated during emergency use.
The patient compartment is the most dangerous seat, and unrestrained rear occupants account for most serious injuries.
Intersections and backing dominate crash types; complete stops and a spotter prevent most of both.
Lights and siren save only about 1.7 to 3.6 minutes on a typical call, which rarely justifies the added risk.
Exemptions are conditional on due regard; right of way is not a legal defense after a collision.

checks.q: Where do occupant deaths and serious injuries in ambulance crashes concentrate?
choices: The driver's seat
The front passenger seat
The patient compartment, among unrestrained occupants
Outside the vehicle
checks.why: Unrestrained rear occupants become projectiles. This is why current ambulance designs use crash-tested, forward-facing seating with restraints.

checks.q: What must an ambulance operator do at a red light while running lights and siren?
choices: Slow and proceed if traffic appears clear
Come to a complete stop and clear the intersection lane by lane
Sound an air horn and proceed
Proceed at the posted speed limit
checks.why: Exemptions allow proceeding after stopping, not through without stopping. Clearing lane by lane with eye contact is what prevents the classic intersection crash.

checks.q: You are backing the ambulance and lose sight of your spotter in the mirror. What do you do?
choices: Continue slowly
Sound the horn and continue
Stop immediately until the spotter is visible again
Ask the spotter to shout directions
checks.why: Losing visual contact means you no longer know what is behind you. Stopping immediately is the rule that makes the spotter system work.

lessons.title: Fatigue, sleep, and lasting in this career
lessons.body:
## Sleep loss is a clinical impairment

The brain does not tolerate sleep debt the way people believe it does. Being awake for about **17 to 19 hours** produces performance decrements comparable to a blood alcohol concentration of roughly `0.05%`. Around **24 hours** awake, the comparison is closer to `0.10%`, which is above the legal driving limit in every state.

Two other mechanisms matter on a night shift. **Circadian nadir**: body temperature, alertness, and reaction time bottom out between roughly `0200` and `0600` regardless of how much you slept, which is why errors and crashes cluster there. **Microsleeps**: involuntary lapses lasting a few seconds that the person does not notice, which is exactly long enough to cross a center line.

Chronic partial sleep loss compounds. Sleeping `6` hours a night for two weeks produces impairment similar to a full night without sleep, and the people in those studies rated themselves as only slightly tired. **Self-assessment of impairment fails precisely when impairment is highest.**

## What the EMS fatigue guidelines actually recommend

An evidence-based guideline effort for EMS fatigue risk management produced a short list of recommendations, and they are worth knowing because they are testable and practical:

- Use **validated fatigue and sleepiness surveys** to measure, rather than guessing.
- Prefer **shifts shorter than 24 hours** where staffing allows.
- Provide access to **caffeine** as a fatigue countermeasure.
- Allow **napping on duty**.
- Provide **education and training** on sleep health and fatigue.

## Using the countermeasures correctly

**Naps.** `20` to `30` minutes avoids deep sleep and the grogginess that follows waking from it (sleep inertia). If you sleep longer, allow `15` to `30` minutes to become fully functional before driving or making decisions. A nap before a night shift is more useful than coffee during it.

**Caffeine.** `100` to `200 mg`, about one to two cups of coffee, takes roughly `15` to `30` minutes to work and has a half-life of about `5` hours. That means a dose at `0300` is still half in your system at `0800` when you are trying to sleep. Front-load the shift, stop several hours before you intend to sleep, and do not use it continuously, because tolerance removes the benefit.

**Light.** Bright light during the night shift and dark, cool, quiet conditions during daytime sleep are the strongest circadian levers available. Sunglasses on the drive home genuinely help.

**The commute.** Driving home after a night shift is one of the highest-risk things EMS providers do. If you are fighting to stay awake, pull over for a `20`-minute nap or call someone. It is not dramatic; it is arithmetic.

## The rest of staying in the career

**Stress** arrives acutely during a call, delayed a few days later, and cumulatively as burnout. Warning signs are irritability, sleep change, isolation, cynicism about patients, and increased drinking.

Support that works: peer support programs, employee assistance programs, and clinicians who understand first-responder work. Single-session mandatory debriefings have mixed evidence; voluntary peer support and real access to care are what current guidance emphasizes.

The numbers that should prompt action rather than shame: EMS providers are injured on the job at roughly three times the rate of the average worker, back injuries are the leading cause of career-ending disability, and a widely cited national survey found about `37%` of EMS providers had contemplated suicide and `6.6%` had attempted it. The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is available by call or text, and many regions have dedicated first-responder support lines.

> **Key:** You cannot accurately judge your own impairment when you are impaired. Use rules set in advance, not in-the-moment judgment.

> **On shift:** Hydration, a real meal, a `20`-minute nap when permitted, and a plan for the drive home do more for your performance at hour 19 than willpower does.
keyPoints: 17 to 19 hours awake impairs performance like a blood alcohol of about 0.05 percent; 24 hours is closer to 0.10 percent.
The circadian nadir between 0200 and 0600 degrades alertness regardless of prior sleep.
EMS fatigue guidelines recommend measuring fatigue, shifts under 24 hours, caffeine access, on-duty napping, and education.
Naps of 20 to 30 minutes avoid sleep inertia; caffeine has a half-life of about 5 hours, so late doses ruin daytime sleep.
The post-night-shift commute is a documented high-risk activity, and self-assessment of impairment is least reliable when impairment is highest.

checks.q: Being awake for about 24 hours produces impairment comparable to what blood alcohol concentration?
choices: 0.02 percent
0.05 percent
0.10 percent
0.20 percent
checks.why: About 17 to 19 hours awake resembles 0.05 percent and roughly 24 hours resembles 0.10 percent, which is above the legal driving limit everywhere.

checks.q: Why is a 20 to 30 minute nap preferred over a 90 minute nap on duty?
choices: It provides more restorative sleep
It avoids deep sleep and the grogginess of sleep inertia on waking
It is required by federal rule
Longer naps have no effect
checks.why: Short naps stay out of deep sleep, so you wake functional. Waking from deep sleep needs 15 to 30 minutes before driving or decision making.

checks.q: Caffeine taken at 0300 is still meaningfully present at what time, given a half-life of about 5 hours?
choices: It clears within an hour
checks.why: Roughly half the dose remains around 0800, which is exactly when a night-shift provider is trying to fall asleep. Front-load caffeine and stop hours before sleep.

lessons.title: Community paramedicine and the evidence behind it
lessons.body:
## Why a service built for emergencies started making house calls

A sizeable fraction of 911 calls are not emergencies, and a small number of people generate a large share of them. Traditional EMS answers each call in isolation, transports, and repeats the cycle next week. **Mobile integrated healthcare and community paramedicine (MIH-CP)** is the attempt to break that loop by sending a trained provider to the problem before it becomes a call.

## What these programs actually do

- **Post-discharge visits** within 24 to 72 hours for patients at high risk of readmission, especially heart failure, chronic lung disease, and after major surgery.
- **Medication reconciliation:** looking in the cabinet, comparing it to the discharge list, and finding the duplicate, the expired bottle, and the medication never filled.
- **Chronic disease checks:** weights in heart failure patients, blood pressure, blood glucose, wound checks.
- **Home safety assessment:** the loose rug, the missing grab bar, the stairs with no rail, which is primary prevention for the fall that would have been next month's call.
- **Frequent-caller case management,** connecting a person to primary care, behavioral health, housing, or food resources instead of an emergency department.
- **Alternative destinations and treat-in-place** where regulation and medical direction permit, sending a patient to urgent care, a clinic, or a crisis center rather than an emergency department.
- **Telemedicine in the field**, connecting a physician to the patient's kitchen.

Programs are staffed by paramedics and sometimes EMTs with additional training, always under physician medical direction, and usually in partnership with a hospital, a health system, or an insurer.

## The obstacles are structural, not clinical

The traditional payment model reimburses **transport**, not care, so a program that successfully keeps someone home may generate no revenue. State scope-of-practice rules were written for emergency response and often do not describe a home visit. And the systems that must share data, meaning EMS, hospital, and primary care, frequently cannot.

## Reading the evidence behind any of it

MIH-CP is sold with outcome claims, which makes it a good place to practice evaluating them.

**Study strength, weakest to strongest:** case report, case series, case-control, cohort, randomized controlled trial, systematic review and meta-analysis. Randomization matters because it balances the things you did not think to measure; without it, sicker or healthier patients may have selected themselves into one group.

**Five questions for any study:**

1. What was the design, and were patients randomized?
2. Who was included and excluded, and do my patients resemble them?
3. What was the outcome measured, and is it one that matters to a patient? Survival and function matter; a laboratory value or a surrogate marker may not.
4. How large was the effect in **absolute** terms?
5. Who funded it, and was the analysis preplanned?

**The statistics worth knowing:**

- A **p value** under `0.05` means the result is unlikely to be chance alone. It says nothing about whether the effect is large or clinically useful.
- A **confidence interval** shows the range of plausible values. A 95 percent interval that crosses "no effect" means the study did not establish one.
- **Relative risk reduction** inflates impressions. Dropping from `2%` to `1%` is a `50%` relative reduction and a `1%` absolute reduction.
- **Number needed to treat (NNT)** is `1` divided by the absolute risk reduction. A `1%` absolute reduction means `100` patients treated for one to benefit.
- **Sensitivity** is how well a test catches disease, so a highly sensitive test is good for ruling out. **Specificity** is how well it excludes people without disease, so a highly specific test is good for ruling in.
- **Correlation is not causation.** This is why practices supported for decades by observational data, such as routine long backboard use and pneumatic anti-shock garments, faded once they were studied properly.

> **Key:** Ask for the absolute numbers. Relative percentages are how weak effects are made to sound decisive.

> **On the exam:** A study without randomization cannot exclude confounding, and that is the standard answer to "what is the main limitation."
keyPoints: Mobile integrated healthcare and community paramedicine send providers to problems before they become 911 calls.
Typical services include post-discharge visits, medication reconciliation, home safety checks, frequent-caller case management, and alternative destinations.
The main barriers are payment tied to transport, scope rules written for emergencies, and data that does not cross systems.
Evidence strength runs case report to case series to cohort to randomized trial to systematic review; randomization controls unmeasured confounders.
Judge effects in absolute terms and by number needed to treat, since relative risk reduction exaggerates small effects.

checks.q: A program reports that readmissions fell from 4 percent to 2 percent. How should this be described?
choices: A 50 percent reduction, which is a large clinical effect
A 2 percent absolute reduction, number needed to treat 50
A 2 percent relative reduction
An effect that cannot be quantified
checks.why: The absolute reduction is 2 percentage points, so the number needed to treat is 1 divided by 0.02, or 50. The 50 percent relative figure describes the same data far more dramatically.

checks.q: What is the main limitation of a study where patients were not randomly assigned?
choices: The sample size is always too small
Confounding cannot be excluded, so the groups may have differed in ways nobody measured
The p value cannot be calculated
It cannot be published
checks.why: Randomization is what balances unmeasured differences between groups. Without it, an apparent effect may be explained by who ended up in which group.

checks.q: What is the biggest structural obstacle to community paramedicine programs?
choices: Lack of clinical skills among paramedics
Payment models that reimburse transport rather than care delivered without transport
Patient refusal to participate
Absence of medical direction
checks.why: A program that succeeds by keeping patients home may generate no revenue under transport-based reimbursement. Scope rules and data sharing are the other structural barriers.

lessons.title: New Jersey EMS: tiers, direction, and reporting
lessons.body:
## The state agency and your certificate

EMS in New Jersey is regulated by the **Office of Emergency Medical Services (OEMS)** within the New Jersey Department of Health. OEMS certifies EMTs, licenses ambulance services and mobile intensive care programs, and sets the training and reporting requirements. New Jersey uses the National Registry cognitive examination for initial EMT certification, with the state certificate issued on a multi-year cycle and continuing education required for renewal. Requirement details change, so confirm current hours and cycle length with OEMS rather than with a classmate.

The regulatory chapters worth recognizing by name: ambulance and invalid coach services are governed under **N.J.A.C. 8:40**, mobile intensive care (ALS) programs under **N.J.A.C. 8:41**, and specialty care transport under its own subchapter.

## The two-tier system, and why it changes your calls

New Jersey separates BLS from ALS by vehicle and by employer.

- **BLS** is delivered by EMT-staffed transporting ambulances, run by volunteer first aid squads, municipal and county services, and hospital-based or contracted providers.
- **ALS** is delivered by hospital-based **Mobile Intensive Care Units (MICUs)**, staffed by Mobile Intensive Care Paramedics operating from **non-transporting fly cars**. New Jersey does not use the AEMT level in its normal system design.

So the paramedic is usually not on your ambulance. The operational consequences are permanent features of working here:

1. **Request ALS early**, because the MICU is coming from a hospital base that may be several towns away.
2. **Do not sit still waiting.** Begin transport toward the receiving facility and arrange an intercept en route.
3. **The paramedic decides whether to ride in.** After assessing, the MICU crew either accompanies the patient in your ambulance or releases the patient to BLS care and clears.
4. **You keep working.** ALS presence does not convert you into a bystander; the BLS crew still drives, documents, and assists.

## When to request an intercept

Criteria vary by county and by regional protocol, but the presentations that routinely warrant ALS are consistent:

- Cardiac arrest, or return of circulation after arrest
- Chest pain or other presentation suspicious for acute coronary syndrome
- Respiratory distress not resolving with BLS measures
- Altered mental status, unresponsiveness, or suspected stroke
- Active seizure or repeated seizures
- Anaphylaxis, or any airway compromise
- Major trauma meeting trauma-center criteria
- Shock or significant hypotension from any cause
- Overdose or poisoning with airway, breathing, or circulatory compromise
- Obstetric emergencies with complications

The honest rule: if you are wondering whether to call, call. Canceling a MICU costs nothing.

## Medical direction and the BLS toolkit

You operate under statewide and regional BLS protocols issued through OEMS and your agency's medical director. New Jersey EMTs commonly carry and use oxygen, suction, airway adjuncts, an AED, glucometry, oral glucose, aspirin, and **naloxone**, which New Jersey authorized broadly for EMTs following the Overdose Prevention Act, and epinephrine auto-injectors under approved programs. EMTs also assist patients with their own prescribed nitroglycerin, metered-dose inhaler, or auto-injector. Some agencies carry CPAP and other additions with medical director and OEMS approval. Because this list has changed repeatedly, verify your agency's current protocol rather than trusting a textbook.

## Reporting obligations

- **Every patient contact generates a patient care report**, and agencies submit run data into the state EMS data system, which feeds the national EMS database (NEMSIS).
- **Suspected child abuse or neglect:** New Jersey is a universal mandated reporting state. Any person with reasonable cause must report immediately to the State Central Registry at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE.
- **Suspected abuse of a vulnerable adult** goes to county Adult Protective Services.
- **Occupational exposures** go to your designated infection control officer immediately, which is how notification from the receiving facility is triggered.
- **Gunshot and stab wounds, certain communicable diseases, and specified incidents** are reported per state law and agency policy.

> **Key:** In New Jersey the medic arrives separately. Request early, move toward the hospital, and intercept on the way.

> **On the exam:** National questions assume a paramedic may be on the ambulance. New Jersey questions assume an intercept model with hospital-based MICUs and no AEMT tier.
keyPoints: New Jersey OEMS, within the Department of Health, certifies EMTs and licenses ambulance and mobile intensive care services.
The state is two-tier: EMT-staffed transporting BLS units and hospital-based MICU paramedics in non-transporting fly cars, with no AEMT tier in normal use.
Request ALS early and begin transport toward the hospital rather than waiting in place for the intercept.
The MICU crew assesses and then either rides in or releases the patient back to BLS care.
Mandated reporting includes child abuse to 1-877-NJ-ABUSE, vulnerable adult abuse to Adult Protective Services, and exposures to the designated infection control officer.

checks.q: In New Jersey, how does a paramedic normally reach your patient?
choices: As the second crew member on your ambulance
In a non-transporting fly car from a hospital-based MICU program
By helicopter only
Dispatched from the receiving emergency department on foot
checks.why: New Jersey ALS is hospital-based and non-transporting. Paramedics respond separately and either ride in or release the patient to BLS.

checks.q: You have a patient who needs ALS and the MICU is 8 minutes out while the hospital is 11 minutes away. What is the best action?
choices: Stay on scene until the MICU arrives
Cancel ALS and transport without notifying anyone
Begin transport toward the hospital and arrange an intercept en route
Transport at emergency speed without ALS
checks.why: Moving toward definitive care while the MICU meets you on the way uses both resources. Sitting still spends the intercept time for nothing.

checks.q: Which agency certifies New Jersey EMTs and licenses ambulance services?
choices: The National Registry of EMTs
The Office of Emergency Medical Services within the Department of Health
The Department of Transportation
The county prosecutor's office
checks.why: OEMS is the state regulator. The National Registry supplies the cognitive examination used for initial certification but does not issue the state certificate.

cards.front: What four purposes does a single patient care report serve?
cards.back: Clinical handoff, legal record, billing document, and data submission to the state and national EMS databases.

cards.front: What does the CHART narrative format stand for?
cards.back: Chief complaint, History, Assessment, Rx meaning treatment, and Transport. Using one format every call prevents dropped sections under pressure.

cards.front: What does the SOAP narrative format stand for?
cards.back: Subjective what the patient reports, Objective what you measured and observed, Assessment your impression, and Plan what you did and where you went.

cards.front: Which times belong in the run data of every PCR?
cards.back: Dispatch, en route, on scene, patient contact, scene departure, arrival at facility, and transfer of care, plus mileage and destination.

cards.front: How do you document an intervention you deliberately withheld?
cards.back: State the intervention and the clinical reason, such as 'oral glucose withheld due to inability to protect airway.' A reasoned omission is an assessment finding.

cards.front: What is medical necessity in a PCR and how do you document it?
cards.back: Why this patient required ambulance transport rather than another means, stated as a clinical fact: unable to ambulate due to open femur deformity, or unable to protect airway.

cards.front: Protocol says every trauma patient gets oxygen and you did not apply it. What do you chart?
cards.back: What actually happened, plus the reason if you had one. Charting an intervention you did not perform is falsification and ends certifications.

cards.front: Which negligence element is missing when a provider errs but the patient is unharmed?
cards.back: Damages. All four elements, duty, breach, damages, and causation, must be present, so breach without harm is a quality issue rather than a claim.

cards.front: Why does 'the patient signed the refusal' fail as a defense?
cards.back: The signature proves nothing about capacity or about whether risks were explained. The chart must show the capacity determination, the risks named, alternatives offered, and medical direction contact.

cards.front: When does a transfer of care become abandonment?
cards.back: When the receiving provider is at a lower level than the patient's needs require, or when no one has actually accepted care. Direction of transfer is the test.

cards.front: Distinguish assault, battery, and false imprisonment in EMS.
cards.back: Assault is placing someone in fear of unwanted contact. Battery is the unconsented touching. False imprisonment is confining or transporting a competent refusing adult.

cards.front: What four conditions do Good Samaritan statutes generally require?
cards.back: The care is voluntary, in good faith, without expectation of payment, and within the scope of the responder's training. They do not cover gross negligence.

cards.front: A bystander physician directs care outside your protocol. What do you do?
cards.back: Stay within your scope and contact online medical direction so the physicians resolve it. A physician on scene is typically required to show credentials, accept responsibility, and accompany the patient.

cards.front: What does implied consent cover, and what does it not?
cards.back: It covers emergency care for a patient who cannot consent, limited to what the emergency requires. It does not authorize non-emergency treatment or override a valid advance directive.

cards.front: What does SALT stand for?
cards.back: Sort, Assess, Lifesaving interventions, Treatment and transport. It is the national consensus mass casualty triage model.

cards.front: How does SALT sort patients before individual assessment?
cards.back: Two voice commands. Those who walk to a designated area are assessed third; those who wave or move purposefully are second; the still and silent are assessed first.

cards.front: Which lifesaving interventions are permitted during SALT triage?
cards.back: Control major hemorrhage, open the airway by positioning with 2 rescue breaths for a child, chest decompression, and auto-injector antidotes, all within scope.

cards.front: Name the five SALT categories.
cards.back: Immediate (red), Delayed (yellow), Minimal (green), Expectant (gray), and Dead (black). Expectant reflects available resources and is revisited as resources grow.

cards.front: How does SALT differ in philosophy from START?
cards.back: START sorts by who can walk and by physiology alone. SALT assesses the still and silent first, permits a short list of lifesaving interventions during triage, and adds an expectant category.

cards.front: What should the transport officer ask each hospital for?
cards.back: Capacity by category, such as two immediate, four delayed, ten minimal, rather than a general yes or no on taking patients.

cards.front: Why must the closest hospital be warned specifically at an MCI?
cards.back: A large share of walking wounded self-transport by car or on foot to the nearest facility before the first ambulance arrives, arriving uncounted and untriaged.

cards.front: List the decontamination sequence in order.
cards.back: Triage at entry, remove clothing, brush dry material, flush with low-pressure warm water, soap for oily agents, irrigate eyes, dry and cover, then treat in the cold zone.

cards.front: Why low-pressure warm water rather than high-pressure or cold?
cards.back: High pressure drives contaminant into skin and abrades it. Cold water causes hypothermia in a naked wet patient, a common complication of mass decontamination.

cards.front: Why are dry chemicals brushed off before flushing?
cards.back: Some dry chemicals react violently with water. Brushing removes bulk material before any liquid is introduced.

cards.front: How do vesicant and pulmonary agent exposures differ in timing?
cards.back: Vesicants such as mustard cause delayed blistering hours later. Pulmonary agents such as chlorine and phosgene cause immediate irritation with delayed pulmonary edema.

cards.front: Why does chlorine gas collect in basements and low ground?
cards.back: It is heavier than air, so it settles rather than dispersing upward. Approach from uphill and upwind and keep patients out of low areas.

cards.front: What are the three protections against radiation exposure?
cards.back: Time, distance, and shielding. Minimize time near the source, maximize distance, and put mass between you and it. A decontaminated irradiated patient poses little risk.

cards.front: What are the four phases of blast injury?
cards.back: Primary from the pressure wave on air-filled organs, secondary from flying fragments (most casualties), tertiary from the body being thrown, quaternary from burns, crush, and inhalation.

cards.front: Roughly how many ambulance crashes occur annually in the United States?
cards.back: Estimates run about 4,500 to 6,500 per year, with roughly 30 fatal crashes annually and thousands of injuries.

cards.front: Which seat in an ambulance is most dangerous in a crash?
cards.back: The patient compartment. Serious injuries and deaths concentrate among unrestrained rear occupants, who become projectiles.

cards.front: What is the wake effect?
cards.back: Crashes that occur behind a responding emergency vehicle among drivers reacting to its passage. Some studies suggest these may outnumber ambulance crashes themselves.

cards.front: What are the five intersection rules for emergency driving?
cards.back: Complete stop at every red light and stop sign, clear lane by lane, make eye contact, change the siren tone on approach, and assume you are neither seen nor heard.

cards.front: What is the spotter rule when backing an ambulance?
cards.back: A spotter at the rear corner visible in your mirror with agreed signals, and you stop the instant you lose sight of them. With no spotter, get out and walk the path.

cards.front: Do lights and sirens grant immunity from traffic law?
cards.back: No. They grant conditional exemptions, and the legal standard remains due regard for everyone else's safety. Right of way is not a defense after a crash.

cards.front: Why do current ambulance designs avoid side-facing bench seats?
cards.back: Crash testing showed poor occupant protection. Newer patient compartments use forward-facing, crash-tested seating with restraints.

cards.front: How does 17 to 19 hours awake compare to alcohol impairment?
cards.back: Performance decrements comparable to a blood alcohol of about 0.05 percent. At roughly 24 hours awake the comparison is closer to 0.10 percent.

cards.front: What is the circadian nadir and when does it occur?
cards.back: The daily low point in alertness, temperature, and reaction time, roughly between 0200 and 0600, which occurs regardless of prior sleep.

cards.front: What are the five EMS fatigue risk management recommendations?
cards.back: Measure fatigue with validated surveys, use shifts shorter than 24 hours, provide caffeine access, permit on-duty napping, and provide sleep health education.

cards.front: Why cap an on-duty nap at 20 to 30 minutes?
cards.back: It stays out of deep sleep, so you wake functional. Waking from deep sleep produces sleep inertia requiring 15 to 30 minutes before driving or deciding.

cards.front: What is caffeine's half-life and why does it matter on nights?
cards.back: About 5 hours, so a 0300 dose is half present at 0800 when you are trying to sleep. Front-load the shift and stop hours before sleep.

cards.front: Why can't you rely on self-assessment of fatigue?
cards.back: Accuracy of self-assessment falls as impairment rises, and microsleeps go unnoticed by the person having them. Use rules set in advance instead.

cards.front: What suicide-related figures were reported in a national EMS provider survey?
cards.back: About 37 percent reported having contemplated suicide and 6.6 percent reported an attempt, far above general population rates. The 988 line is available by call or text.

cards.front: What does mobile integrated healthcare and community paramedicine do?
cards.back: Post-discharge visits, medication reconciliation, chronic disease and home safety checks, frequent-caller case management, alternative destinations, and field telemedicine, under medical direction.

cards.front: What are the three structural barriers to community paramedicine?
cards.back: Payment models that reimburse transport rather than care, scope-of-practice rules written for emergency response, and data systems that do not share across EMS, hospital, and primary care.

cards.front: Rank study designs from weakest to strongest evidence.
cards.back: Case report, case series, case-control, cohort, randomized controlled trial, then systematic review and meta-analysis.

cards.front: What does a p value under 0.05 actually tell you?
cards.back: That the result is unlikely to be due to chance alone. It says nothing about the size of the effect or whether it matters clinically.

cards.front: How do you calculate number needed to treat?
cards.back: 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction. A drop from 4 percent to 2 percent is a 2 percent absolute reduction, so the NNT is 50.

cards.front: Why is relative risk reduction misleading?
cards.back: It hides the baseline. Going from 2 percent to 1 percent is a 50 percent relative reduction but only a 1 percent absolute reduction, meaning 100 treated for one to benefit.

cards.front: Sensitivity versus specificity: which rules out and which rules in?
cards.back: A highly sensitive test catches nearly all disease, so a negative helps rule out. A highly specific test rarely flags healthy people, so a positive helps rule in.

cards.front: Which agency certifies EMTs and licenses ambulance services in New Jersey?
cards.back: The Office of Emergency Medical Services (OEMS) within the New Jersey Department of Health. The National Registry supplies the initial cognitive exam.

cards.front: How is ALS structured in New Jersey?
cards.back: Hospital-based Mobile Intensive Care Units staffed by Mobile Intensive Care Paramedics in non-transporting fly cars that intercept BLS ambulances. There is no routine AEMT tier.

cards.front: What do you do while waiting for a New Jersey ALS intercept?
cards.back: Do not wait in place. Begin transport toward the receiving facility and arrange to meet the MICU en route; canceling a MICU costs nothing.

cards.front: What happens when the MICU crew arrives at your patient?
cards.back: They assess and then either ride in with the patient in your ambulance or release the patient back to BLS care and clear. The BLS crew keeps working either way.

cards.front: Name six presentations that routinely warrant an ALS intercept.
cards.back: Cardiac arrest, suspected acute coronary syndrome, respiratory distress unresolved by BLS, altered mental status or suspected stroke, active seizure, and major trauma or shock.

cards.front: Which regulatory chapters govern New Jersey ambulance and ALS services?
cards.back: N.J.A.C. 8:40 covers ambulance and invalid coach services, and N.J.A.C. 8:41 covers mobile intensive care programs, with specialty care transport under its own subchapter.

cards.front: List four New Jersey EMS reporting obligations.
cards.back: A patient care report for every contact submitted to the state data system, child abuse to 1-877-NJ-ABUSE, vulnerable adult abuse to Adult Protective Services, and exposures to your infection control officer.

quiz.q: You deliberately withheld oral glucose from an unresponsive hypoglycemic patient. What is the best documentation?
choices: Oral glucose withheld due to inability to protect airway; ALS requested for dextrose
Oral glucose not given
Patient could not take glucose
Glucose given per protocol
quiz.why: It records the clinical reasoning and the alternative action. A blank omission looks like forgetfulness, and documenting glucose that was not given is falsification.

quiz.q: Which element is required for a PCR to support medical necessity for ambulance transport?
choices: The patient's insurance carrier
The crew's certification numbers
A clinical statement of why other transportation was not appropriate
The receiving hospital's bed number
quiz.why: Medical necessity is established by describing the patient's condition, such as inability to ambulate or to protect the airway. The other items belong in the chart but do not establish necessity.

quiz.q: Your agency's protocol requires oxygen on all trauma patients, but you did not apply it during a short transport. What must the PCR say?
choices: That oxygen was applied per protocol
Exactly what happened, with your clinical reason if you had one
Nothing, to avoid drawing attention
That the patient declined oxygen
quiz.why: Falsifying a chart to match a protocol is fraud and is far more serious than a protocol deviation. Record the facts and the reason.

quiz.q: Which set of times is the minimum needed to reconstruct a call years later?
choices: Dispatch time only
Arrival and departure only
Patient contact only
Dispatch, en route, on scene, patient contact, departure, facility arrival, and transfer of care
quiz.why: The full time set establishes response interval, scene time, transport time, and when care was accepted. Any single time proves nothing about the sequence.

quiz.q: An EMT fails to check a blood glucose on an altered patient labeled as intoxicated. The patient is later found with a glucose of 28 mg/dL and suffers permanent injury. Which element of negligence is most clearly established by the missed glucose check?
choices: Breach of the standard of care
Duty to act
Damages
Causation
quiz.why: Duty existed from dispatch and damages are evident, but the missed glucose specifically demonstrates failure to act as a reasonably prudent EMT, which is breach.

quiz.q: An EMT is dismissive and sarcastic during a call but performs every clinical step correctly and the patient does well. What is the most accurate characterization?
choices: Negligence, because professional conduct was breached
Battery
A conduct complaint, but not negligence, because no damages were caused
Abandonment
quiz.why: Negligence requires damages caused by a clinical breach. Poor bedside manner is a legitimate complaint and discipline matter, but it is not a tort without harm.

quiz.q: A competent adult clearly refuses an intervention and the EMT performs it anyway believing it is in the patient's interest. What has occurred?
choices: Assault
Battery
False imprisonment
Implied consent
quiz.why: Battery is the unconsented touching. Assault would be the threat alone, and false imprisonment would require confining or transporting the refusing patient.

quiz.q: A paramedic managing a patient with an IV infusion and a cardiac monitor decides to release the patient to the BLS crew because a higher priority call came in. What is this?
choices: Appropriate resource management
Permitted with online medical direction
A protocol deviation only
Abandonment, because the receiving level cannot meet the patient's needs
quiz.why: Transfer must be to an equal or higher level when the patient requires interventions outside the receiving provider's scope. Operational pressure does not change that.

quiz.q: An off-duty EMT stops at a crash, provides care within her training, accepts no payment, and is later sued for an imperfect splint. What is the likely analysis?
choices: Good Samaritan protection generally applies, because the care was voluntary, in good faith, unpaid, and within training
Good Samaritan laws never apply to certified providers
She is liable because she had a duty to act
She is protected even if she performed a procedure far outside her training
quiz.why: Those four conditions are exactly what Good Samaritan statutes protect. They do not, however, cover gross negligence or acts far outside the responder's training.

quiz.q: Under SALT triage, which patients are assessed first?
choices: Those who walked to the designated collection area
Those who are still and silent or have an obvious life threat
Those who waved or moved purposefully
Children under 8 years old
quiz.why: SALT sorts by likelihood of dying now. The still and silent are assessed first, then those who waved, then those who walked.

quiz.q: During SALT individual assessment you find a patient with severe arterial bleeding from an arm. What may you do?
choices: Nothing; triage prohibits all interventions
Splint the arm and move on
Apply a tourniquet, because hemorrhage control is a permitted lifesaving intervention
Start an IV and give fluids
quiz.why: SALT permits hemorrhage control, airway opening with rescue breaths for children, chest decompression, and auto-injector antidotes. Splinting and IV therapy are treatment, not triage.

quiz.q: What does the expectant (gray) category in SALT represent?
choices: Patients who are already dead
Patients with only minor injuries
Patients who refused care
Patients unlikely to survive given the resources currently available, who receive comfort care and are reassessed
quiz.why: Expectant is a resource judgment, not a verdict on the patient. As resources arrive, an expectant patient may be re-categorized as immediate.

quiz.q: You are the transport officer at a 40-patient incident. What question should you ask each hospital?
choices: How many immediate, delayed, and minimal patients can you accept right now?
Can you take patients?
How many beds are open in the hospital?
What is your average wait time?
quiz.why: A facility may absorb many minimal patients but only one immediate. Category-specific capacity is what prevents saturating a single resuscitation resource.

quiz.q: At a large incident near a hospital, what should you specifically warn the closest facility about?
choices: That the incident commander will call them directly
That they should stop accepting routine patients
That uncounted walking wounded will likely arrive on their own before any ambulance
That they should send staff to the scene
quiz.why: In real mass casualty incidents a large share of minor patients self-transport by car or on foot to the nearest hospital, arriving untriaged and unregistered.

quiz.q: Which decontamination step removes the largest share of contaminant?
choices: Soap and scrub brush application
Removing and bagging the patient's clothing
Eye irrigation with saline
Application of a neutralizing agent
quiz.why: Clothing removal eliminates roughly 80 to 90 percent of contaminant and is the first action after triage at the decon entry. Neutralizing agents are generally not used on skin.

quiz.q: A patient is covered in a dry powdered chemical. What is the correct first action?
choices: Flush immediately with high-pressure water
Apply a neutralizing solution
Cover the powder with a dressing
Brush the dry material off before any water is applied
quiz.why: Some dry chemicals react violently with water, so bulk material is brushed away first. High pressure also drives contaminant into skin.

quiz.q: Five patients from a warehouse basement have burning eyes, coughing, and a bleach-like odor on their clothes. Which agent is most consistent, and what does it imply about the scene?
choices: A nerve agent, so expect pinpoint pupils in responders
A vesicant, so expect immediate blistering
Chlorine, which is heavier than air and pools in low areas such as basements
A biological agent, so expect delayed onset over days
quiz.why: Chlorine smells like bleach, irritates immediately, and is heavier than air, so it collects in basements and low ground. Vesicant blistering is delayed and biological agents have no immediate scene.

quiz.q: In an explosion with many casualties, which blast injury phase produces the greatest number of patients?
choices: Secondary, from flying fragments and debris
Primary, from the pressure wave
Tertiary, from being thrown against objects
Quaternary, from burns and inhalation
quiz.why: Fragmentation injuries account for the largest casualty numbers. Primary blast injury to lungs, ears, and bowel is the most distinctive but affects fewer patients.

quiz.q: Which statement about ambulance crash patterns is correct?
choices: Most serious crashes occur while returning to quarters without lights
Serious injuries and deaths concentrate among unrestrained occupants in the patient compartment
The driver's seat is the most dangerous position
Backing collisions are rare
quiz.why: The rear compartment is the most dangerous seat, most serious crashes occur during emergency use, and backing is the most frequent collision type overall.

quiz.q: You are responding with lights and siren and approach a red light at a busy intersection. What is required?
choices: Slow to 15 miles per hour and proceed
Sound the air horn and proceed at reduced speed
Proceed if the cross traffic appears to be stopping
Come to a complete stop and clear the intersection lane by lane
quiz.why: Exemptions permit proceeding after stopping, not without stopping. Clearing lane by lane with eye contact is what prevents the classic intersection collision.

quiz.q: During backing, your spotter disappears from your mirror view. What is the correct action?
choices: Stop immediately and do not move until the spotter is visible again
Continue at idle speed
Sound the horn twice and continue
Have your partner shout directions from inside
quiz.why: If you cannot see the spotter, you have no information about what is behind you. Stopping immediately is the rule that makes spotting effective.

quiz.q: An ambulance running lights and siren collides with a car that entered the intersection legally. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The ambulance is immune from liability while responding
Right of way is an absolute defense
Exemptions are conditional on driving with due regard, and the crash will be judged against a reasonable operator standard
Liability depends only on the posted speed limit
quiz.why: Lights and siren grant conditional exemptions, never immunity. Due regard is the legal standard applied after every crash.

quiz.q: You are at hour 22 of a 24-hour shift with almost no sleep. How should you interpret your ability to judge whether you are safe to drive?
choices: Self-assessment becomes more accurate with experience
You are safe as long as you feel alert
A cup of coffee restores baseline performance
Self-assessment is least reliable when impairment is greatest, so a rule set in advance should govern
quiz.why: Sleep-deprived people consistently underestimate their impairment and do not notice microsleeps. Pre-set rules such as mandatory relief or a nap are the safeguard.

quiz.q: Which is a recommendation from evidence-based EMS fatigue risk management guidance?
choices: Mandatory 24-hour shifts to improve continuity
Permitting napping while on duty
Banning caffeine during night shifts
Relying on supervisors to judge crew fatigue by observation
quiz.why: The recommendations include measuring fatigue with validated surveys, shifts under 24 hours, caffeine access, on-duty napping, and education. Observation-based judgment is not among them.

quiz.q: You take 200 mg of caffeine at 0300 on a night shift and plan to sleep at 0900. What is the practical consequence?
choices: Roughly half the dose is still active around 0800, making daytime sleep harder
Caffeine clears completely within two hours
Sleep will be unaffected because tolerance develops
It will improve the quality of your daytime sleep
quiz.why: With a half-life near 5 hours, a 0300 dose is about half present at 0800. Front-load caffeine early in the shift and stop several hours before intended sleep.

quiz.q: A community paramedicine program reports that hospital readmissions fell from 4 percent to 2 percent. How should this be described to a skeptical colleague?
choices: A 2 percent relative reduction, which is trivial
A dramatic 50 percent drop in readmissions
A 2 percentage point absolute reduction, number needed to treat 50
An unquantifiable improvement
quiz.why: The absolute reduction is 2 percentage points, giving an NNT of 1 divided by 0.02, or 50 patients enrolled per readmission prevented. The 50 percent relative figure describes identical data more dramatically.

quiz.q: A retrospective study finds patients who received a prehospital treatment had better survival, but treatment was chosen by the crew rather than randomly assigned. What is the main limitation?
choices: The sample size must be too small
Confounding cannot be excluded, since crews may have chosen the treatment for healthier or sicker patients
The p value cannot be computed
Retrospective studies cannot measure survival
quiz.why: Randomization balances unmeasured differences between groups. Without it, the apparent benefit may reflect who was selected rather than the treatment itself.

quiz.q: Which service is characteristic of a mobile integrated healthcare program rather than traditional 911 response?
choices: Rapid transport of trauma patients to a trauma center
Cardiac arrest resuscitation
Interfacility transfer of a ventilated patient
A scheduled post-discharge home visit with medication reconciliation
quiz.why: MIH programs are scheduled, preventive, and often non-transporting. The other three are conventional emergency or transfer functions.

quiz.q: You are a BLS crew in New Jersey with a suspected stroke patient. The MICU is 9 minutes out; the stroke center is 14 minutes away. What is the best action?
choices: Remain on scene until the MICU arrives
Cancel the MICU and transport without notification
Begin transport toward the stroke center and arrange an intercept en route
Transport to the closest hospital regardless of capability
quiz.why: Moving toward definitive care while the fly car meets you uses both resources. Waiting in place spends the intercept interval for nothing, and stroke care is time-critical.

quiz.q: How does the New Jersey ALS model differ from systems where paramedics staff transporting ambulances?
choices: Paramedics operate from hospital-based MICU fly cars that do not transport and intercept BLS units
Paramedics respond only by helicopter
Every BLS ambulance carries one paramedic
ALS is provided exclusively by AEMTs
quiz.why: New Jersey ALS is hospital-based and non-transporting, so the paramedic intercepts the BLS ambulance and then rides in or releases. The AEMT level is not part of the normal system design.

quiz.q: After the MICU crew assesses your patient, what are the two possible outcomes?
choices: They must always transport the patient in their own vehicle
They either ride in with the patient or release the patient back to BLS care
They assume command of the scene until the hospital is reached
They must contact medical control before leaving
quiz.why: MICU vehicles are non-transporting. After assessing, the paramedics accompany the patient in the ambulance or release the patient to BLS and clear.

quiz.q: You suspect child neglect during a call in New Jersey. What is your obligation?
choices: Report only if you can document physical evidence
Report through your supervisor within 72 hours
Report only if the receiving physician agrees
Report immediately to the State Central Registry, since any person with reasonable cause must report
quiz.why: New Jersey is a universal mandated reporting state. Reasonable suspicion is the threshold, proof is not required, and the report goes directly to 1-877-NJ-ABUSE without waiting for confirmation.

scenarios.title: Three years later: the chart on the stand
scenarios.intro: A case is being reviewed in class. Three years ago, a BLS crew responded to a 57-year-old man who fell from a stepladder, struck his head, and declined transport. He died two days later of a subdural hematoma. His family has sued. You are handed the patient care report and asked, step by step, whether it defends the crew. Decide each question before reading the analysis.

steps.prompt:
The narrative reads, in full: "Pt fell off ladder, hit head, AAOx4, refused transport, signed refusal, advised to see MD."

What is the single biggest problem with this narrative?

choices.text: It is too short to be professional
choices.feedback: Length is not the issue. A short chart can be adequate; this one is missing content, which is a different failure.

choices.text: It shows no assessment, no vital signs, and no evidence of a capacity determination or a risk conversation
