choices.feedback: Correct. You cannot document a refusal on a patient you never documented assessing, and 'AAOx4' is not a capacity determination.

choices.text: It fails to state the patient's insurance status
choices.feedback: Billing information does not defend a refusal. The clinical process is what is missing.

steps.prompt:
The plaintiff argues negligence. Which element will the defense most likely contest successfully, and which will they lose?

Which analysis is correct?

choices.text: Duty is contestable; damages are clear
choices.feedback: Duty is not contestable. The crew was dispatched, responded, and made patient contact, which establishes duty outright.

choices.text: Breach is clear from the chart; causation is where the defense will focus
choices.feedback: Correct. The chart itself demonstrates a breach of the refusal standard. Whether transport would have changed the outcome is the contestable element.

choices.text: Damages are contestable because he died of natural causes
choices.feedback: A traumatic subdural hematoma after a witnessed fall is not a natural cause, and death is unambiguous damages.

steps.prompt:
The crew testifies that they did explain the risks of a head bleed, and that the patient understood and declined anyway. The chart does not say so.

How does this testimony fare?

choices.text: It is strong, because sworn testimony outweighs a written record
choices.feedback: Memory of one call among thousands, three years later, is easy to attack. The contemporaneous record carries far more weight.

choices.text: It is weak, because an undocumented conversation is treated as an unproven one
choices.feedback: Correct. 'If it is not documented, it was not done' is not a slogan in this setting; it is how the record is read.

choices.text: It does not matter, because the refusal form was signed
choices.feedback: The signature proves a form was signed. It does not prove capacity was assessed or that risks were explained.

steps.prompt: You are asked to write the narrative this crew should have written. Which version defends the call?

choices.text: "Pt refused transport against medical advice. Pt is an adult and made his own decision. Nothing further."
choices.feedback: This records a conclusion and nothing else. It is the same chart with more words.

choices.text: "Pt assessed. AAOx4. Vitals within normal limits. Risks explained. Refused. Signed."
choices.feedback: Closer, but 'within normal limits' hides the numbers, 'risks explained' does not say which risks, and there is still no capacity evidence.

choices.text: "Full assessment performed: GCS 15, oriented x4, PERRL, no focal deficit, glucose 96, HR 74, BP 148/86, RR 16, SpO2 98 percent at 1908 and 1922. Takes apixaban. Advised specifically of the risk of delayed intracranial bleeding including death, and that anticoagulation increases that risk. Pt repeated back: 'I get it, I could bleed in my brain and die and I still want to stay home.' Alternatives offered: transport now, call back any time, see his physician today, and a family member to stay overnight and check on him. Online medical direction contacted 1926, Dr. Reyes, who spoke with the patient and concurred he has capacity. Refusal signed by pt and witnessed by Officer Doyle, badge 341, 1931."
choices.feedback: Correct. Assessment with numbers, anticoagulation named, capacity demonstrated in the patient's own words, specific risks, alternatives, medical direction by name and time, and an independent witness.

steps.prompt: One more question from the reviewer. The crew realized two days later that they had never charted the glucose reading they actually obtained. What should they have done?

choices.text: Add a labeled late entry with the date and time of entry, stating the value and when it was obtained
choices.feedback: Correct. A labeled late entry made honestly is acceptable. A late entry disguised as contemporaneous is fraud.

choices.text: Edit the original narrative to include it, since it is true
choices.feedback: Electronic records keep an audit trail, and an undisclosed edit after learning of a bad outcome is the worst possible fact pattern.

choices.text: Leave it out, since adding it now would look suspicious
choices.feedback: Omitting a real finding does not help the patient's record or the crew. A transparent late entry is the correct path.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: a refusal is a clinical procedure with documented steps, and the chart is the only proof any of them happened. Duty and damages were never in doubt here, so the whole case lived in breach and causation, and the original narrative handed the plaintiff breach for free. The defensible version differs not in length but in content: numbers rather than 'within normal limits', the anticoagulant named because it changes the risk, capacity demonstrated by quoting the patient's own words back, the specific risk of death stated, alternatives offered, medical direction named with a time, and an independent witness. Finally, a mistake discovered later is fixed in the open with a labeled late entry. Concealed edits turn a documentation problem into an integrity problem, and integrity problems are the ones that end careers.

scenarios.title: Hour 19: fatigue, the drive, and a landing zone
scenarios.intro: It is 0340 on the nineteenth hour of a 24-hour shift. You have slept about 40 minutes all night. You are dispatched for a single-vehicle rollover on a rural two-lane road, 11 miles out, with one patient reported trapped. Your partner has been driving all night and says he is fine.

steps.prompt:
Your partner heads for the driver's door. You notice he missed the last radio transmission and had to ask dispatch to repeat it twice.

What do you do?

choices.text: Say nothing; he has more seniority and said he is fine
choices.feedback: Self-assessment of fatigue is least reliable when impairment is highest, and two missed transmissions is an objective finding, not an opinion.

choices.text: Name the observation and offer to drive: "You missed that transmission twice. I'm up, let me take this one."
choices.feedback: Correct. Lead with the observation rather than a judgment about him, and offer a solution instead of a complaint.

choices.text: Tell dispatch your crew is out of service for fatigue
choices.feedback: Fatigue relief is legitimate, but a trapped patient is 11 miles away and there is a driver available. Swap seats now, raise the staffing issue after.

steps.prompt:
You are responding with lights and siren on a dark rural road. Ahead is a four-way intersection with a red light, no visible traffic, and a hedge blocking the view to the right.

What do you do?

choices.text: Slow to about 20 miles per hour and proceed, since nothing is visible
choices.feedback: The hedge is exactly why 'nothing visible' is not information. Rolling through a red is the most common ambulance crash pattern there is.

choices.text: Come to a complete stop, then clear the intersection lane by lane before proceeding
choices.feedback: Correct. Exemptions allow you to proceed after stopping, never to proceed without stopping, and a blind corner makes lane-by-lane clearing mandatory.

choices.text: Change the siren tone and accelerate through to reduce exposure time
choices.feedback: Changing the tone is right; accelerating through a blind red light is not. Speed increases both the chance of the crash and its severity.

steps.prompt:
On scene: a pickup on its side in a ditch, one occupant trapped, fire is 15 minutes out. Extrication will take time and the nearest trauma center is 48 minutes by ground. A helicopter is available with a 20-minute flight time. There is a flat hayfield 200 feet away with a single line of power poles along the road.

What do you do?

choices.text: Request the helicopter now and begin setting up a landing zone while continuing patient care
choices.feedback: Correct. Prolonged extrication plus a long ground transport plus unstable vitals is the textbook indication, and requests can always be canceled.

choices.text: Wait until the patient is extricated to decide, so you do not waste the aircraft
choices.feedback: The aircraft needs time to launch and arrive. Deciding after extrication wastes exactly the minutes the helicopter was supposed to save.

choices.text: Plan on ground transport since a helicopter adds complexity
choices.feedback: Forty-eight minutes by ground with a patient already showing a narrowing pulse pressure is a poor trade for avoided complexity.

choices.text: Enter the vehicle through the windshield to speed up extrication
choices.feedback: The vehicle is unstabilized and on its side. Complex access is fire's job and entering early risks a second patient.

steps.prompt:
You are setting up the landing zone in the hayfield. A first responder asks what you need.

Which instructions are correct?

choices.text: "Mark a 100 by 100 foot square with weighted cones, keep everyone 100 feet back, secure anything loose, and I'll give the pilot the wire location along the road and the wind direction."
choices.feedback: Correct. Size, weighted markers, a cleared perimeter, and an explicit wire warning are the four things that matter, and wires are the biggest hazard.

choices.text: "Mark the corners with road flares and stand by to guide him in with flashlights."
choices.feedback: Flares near an aircraft and unsecured light sources are both hazards, and nothing that can blow into a rotor belongs in the zone.

choices.text: "Any flat 50 by 50 area is fine at night, just keep the crowd back."
choices.feedback: Fifty feet is half what most helicopters need, and the crowd is not the primary hazard here. The wires are.

choices.text: "Clear the field and let the pilot pick his own spot; he'll see the hazards."
choices.feedback: Pilots rely on ground reports precisely because wires are nearly invisible from the air at night. You owe them the hazard brief.

steps.prompt:
The aircraft lands. The flight crew signals you forward with the patient. The field slopes gently downhill toward the road.

How do you approach?

choices.text: Approach from the rear, where the crew can see you in the mirrors
choices.feedback: The tail rotor is at the rear and is nearly invisible when spinning. Never approach from behind an aircraft.

choices.text: Approach from the front in the pilot's line of sight, and from the downhill side where the main rotor is highest
choices.feedback: Correct. Front approach keeps you visible, and on a slope the downhill side gives the greatest clearance under the main rotor.

choices.text: Approach from the uphill side because the footing is better
choices.feedback: Uphill puts your head closer to the main rotor disc. Footing is managed by moving slowly, not by choosing the dangerous side.

steps.prompt:
The patient is away at 0512. You are back in quarters at 0545 and off duty at 0700. You have a 35-minute drive home and you are fighting your eyes.

What is the right call?

choices.text: Drive home immediately; the sooner you leave the sooner you sleep
choices.feedback: The post-night-shift commute is a documented high-risk activity, and 'sooner' is exactly the reasoning that produces single-vehicle crashes at 0730.

choices.text: Take a 20-minute nap before driving, wear sunglasses on the way, and raise the staffing and shift length issue with your supervisor
choices.feedback: Correct. A short nap avoids sleep inertia, light control helps the circadian shift, and the underlying schedule problem gets addressed through the right channel.

choices.text: Drink two more cups of coffee and drive
choices.feedback: Caffeine at 0700 with a 5-hour half-life will still be working against your daytime sleep at noon, and it does not reverse the reaction-time deficit.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: this call had exactly one clinical decision and five operational ones, and the operational decisions were the dangerous part. Fatigue was addressed by naming an objective observation, two missed transmissions, and offering a fix rather than an opinion. The intersection was handled by the only rule that survives a blind corner at 0350, which is a complete stop and lane-by-lane clearing. The aircraft was requested early because prolonged extrication plus a 48-minute ground transport plus a narrowing pulse pressure is the textbook indication, and a canceled aircraft costs nothing. The landing zone came down to 100 by 100 feet, weighted markers, a cleared perimeter, and an explicit wire warning, because wires are the hazard pilots cannot see. And the shift ended the way it should: a 20-minute nap before a commute that kills more EMS providers than most calls do, and the schedule problem raised with someone who can change it.
